metadataDescription: One star, up close: cut it open, watch it in any light, fly over a sunspot and see a flare break loose.
canvasLabel: The Sun, cut open and watched in any light, with its magnetic field

camera.title: Move the camera
camera.body: Drag to turn, scroll or pinch to zoom.

views.title: Views
views.body: Seven places to stand, from the core to the corona.

light.title: Light
light.body: Explore spectral bands with broad, sometimes multiple temperature responses. Colours are illustrative.

clock.title: Clock
clock.body: Speed up or pause model time. The eruption demonstration has its own playback.

places.title: Places
places.body: Fly to a feature and open its card.

settings.title: Settings
settings.body: Layers, the camera pad and render quality.

guide.title: Guide
guide.body: Learn how the Sun works, step by step.

experiences.title: Viewing modes
experiences.body: Immersive: just the view, no controls. Drift: sit back while the camera flies itself to the music.

viewHints.surface: The photosphere in white light: dark at the limb, boiling with granules, spotted.
viewHints.inside: A quarter cut away: the core, the radiative zone, the tachocline, the convection zone.
viewHints.sunspot: Low over a spot group: the umbra, the penumbra's filaments, granules round them.
viewHints.chromosphere: The limb in Hα: a forest of spicules, plage, filaments and a prominence.
viewHints.corona: The disc hidden, as in an eclipse: streamers, plumes and the wind leaving.
viewHints.eruption: A prescribed eruption and a reduced magnetic cross-section illustrate reconnection.
viewHints.cycle: An idealized repeating cycle illustrates spot migration and polarity reversal; it is not a forecast.

lightNotes.he304: He II + coronal Si XI · synthetic

facts.kCoronaBase: Brightness at the limb, of the disc
facts.cmeSpeed: Mean front speed on chosen timeline

panel.qualityNote: Standard is the Sun as drawn for a desktop; Economy keeps a phone cool.

star.title: The Sun
star.body: A G2 V star of {starMassKg} kg shining {starLuminosityW} W. Its broad visible spectrum appears approximately white to sunlight-adapted eyes. Earth’s atmosphere scatters blue light more strongly, making the sky blue and the low Sun look redder.
star.caution: Colour and brightness are display choices; this is not a calibrated view of solar radiance.

core.title: Core
core.body: Hydrogen fuses into helium, mostly through the proton–proton chain. Nearly all the nuclear energy is generated deep in the core; the marked edge is a luminosity threshold, not a sharp physical boundary.
core.caution: Interior values come from the historical Model S reference model, constrained by solar observations and helioseismology; they are not direct images or a new solar fit.

radiativeZone.title: Radiative zone
radiativeZone.body: Radiation transports energy through this region by repeated interactions with matter, including absorption and re-emission. The diffusion estimate ends at the convection-zone base; it is not the age of an individual photon or the Sun’s thermal response time.
radiativeZone.caution: A model's profile, not a picture.

tachocline.title: Tachocline
tachocline.body: A shear layer near the base of the convection zone separates the nearly uniform rotation of much of the radiative interior from the differentially rotating envelope. It may contribute to the dynamo; the roles of deep, distributed and near-surface processes remain under investigation.
tachocline.caution: Helioseismology constrains this transition. Its thickness, internal field and role in the dynamo are less certain; core rotation is not directly established by this model.

convectionZone.title: Convection zone
convectionZone.body: Buoyant plasma rises, cools and sinks, carrying much of the energy through the outer envelope. Radiation still contributes and ultimately carries energy away from the photosphere.
convectionZone.caution: The plumes drawn are a surrogate for turbulent convection, not a simulation of it.

photosphere.title: Photosphere
photosphere.body: The thin layer where the gas turns transparent and the light escapes. It is darker toward the limb, where sight lines reach only its cooler top.
photosphere.caution: A processed May 2024 HMI mosaic supplies large-scale texture. Limb darkening, colour, close-up detail and subsequent evolution are modelled.

granule.title: Granule
granule.body: The bright top of a rising cell, rimmed by dark lanes where cooled gas sinks. Each lives minutes, and the pattern never stops.
granule.caution: Sizes and lifetimes follow observation; the cells themselves are drawn, not computed.

sunspot.title: Sunspot
sunspot.body: Strong field holds the convection down, so the spot is cooler and looks dark. The umbra is darkest; the penumbra's filaments lean outward.
sunspot.caution: Regions are initialized from NOAA reports associated with the May 2024 HMI mosaic. Their later evolution and fine structure are synthetic.

facula.title: Faculae
facula.body: Bright magnetic structures, especially visible near the limb, compete with dark sunspots. Facular brightening generally wins in the average solar-cycle variation; individual spot passages can temporarily dim the Sun.

chromosphere.title: Chromosphere
chromosphere.body: A dynamic, structured atmosphere above the photosphere. Shocks, waves and magnetic energy release contribute to heating; temperature does not simply rise at every location. Hα reveals plage, filaments and limb structures, but its brightness depends on radiative transfer and atomic populations as well as temperature.
chromosphere.caution: An illustrative Hα view, without optically thick radiative transfer or non-equilibrium ionization.

spicule.title: Spicules
spicule.body: Jets of gas shot up from the chromosphere, each lasting minutes, a forest of them all round the limb.

prominence.title: Prominence
prominence.body: Cool, dense gas held up in the dips of the magnetic field, glowing in Hα above the limb; seen against the disc it is a dark filament.
prominence.caution: A hedgerow prominence authored from observation, not a field solution.

flare.title: Flare
flare.body: Magnetic reconnection can release free magnetic energy above a lower-energy reference field, heating plasma and accelerating particles. The potential background field shown elsewhere does not itself store that free energy.
flare.caution: The cross-section and flow are prescribed. The example GOES class is assigned, not calculated from soft X-ray emission; playback is independent of the main clock.

loops.title: Post-flare loops
loops.body: After a flare the reconnected field fills with hot plasma, an arcade of loops that cools over hours as its gas rains back down.
loops.caution: Here the temperatures and emission are prescribed; cooling, evaporation and coronal rain are not simulated.

corona.title: Corona
corona.body: The tenuous corona is much hotter than the photosphere and emits strongly in extreme ultraviolet and X-rays. Its faint white-light component is sunlight scattered by electrons and dust, best seen when the bright disc is occulted.
corona.caution: Brightness is stretched for the eye; no single exposure shows all of it.

streamer.title: Helmet streamer
streamer.body: Dense plasma on closed magnetic structures forms bright streamers, with extended stalks and surrounding open field. Coronal holes are often dark in coronal EUV bands and commonly feed fast wind; open field does not imply one wind speed.
streamer.caution: Streamers follow the model field, not an observed one.

ejection.title: Coronal mass ejection
ejection.body: An expanding magnetic flux rope carries plasma outward, with a bright front and a darker cavity behind. Its legs can remain connected to the Sun. If it reaches Earth, its field and plasma can drive geomagnetic storms and auroras.

wind.title: Solar wind
wind.body: The hot corona expands into the solar wind. Pressure gradients, waves and magnetic energy release help accelerate it. Fast streams commonly emerge from coronal holes at many latitudes; slow wind has several source regions, including boundaries between open and closed field.
wind.caution: No wind acceleration is solved here; the card gives representative speeds far from the Sun, near Earth’s orbit.

parker.title: Parker Solar Probe
parker.body: Parker first entered the solar corona in April 2021. On 24 December 2024 it reached its record orbit, about {parkerPerihelionR} solar radii from the Sun’s centre at about {parkerSpeed}; later passes repeated this close approach.
parker.caution: A marker for the December 2024 perihelion, not live telemetry. The orbit is not drawn and the probe is not to scale.

core.title: Where the light is made
core.body: Hydrogen fuses in the core, at {coreTemperatureMK} million kelvin and {centralDensity} times the density of water. The energy leaves as light and neutrinos; the neutrinos are out in seconds.

walk.title: The long walk
walk.body: Radiation diffuses through the dense interior while interacting with matter; convection carries much of the energy through the outer envelope. The model’s diffusion estimate to the convection-zone base is {photonWalkKyr} thousand years. Escaping light then reaches Earth in {lightTimeMin} minutes.

dynamo.title: Two rotations
dynamo.body: Much of the radiative interior rotates nearly uniformly. The chosen surface law gives {equatorDays} days at the equator and extrapolates to {poleDays} at the pole, relative to the stars. Shear helps build magnetic field, but the dynamo’s full mechanism and location remain debated.

granules.title: A boiling surface
granules.body: Rising cells about {granuleKm} km across bring the heat up and sink in the dark lanes between them. Each lives about {granuleMin} minutes.

spot.title: Where the field comes through
spot.body: A spot is where a field of up to {spotFieldT} tesla holds the convection down. Cooler by a thousand kelvin, so darker; it only looks black beside the surface.

chromosphere.title: In the light of hydrogen
chromosphere.body: In Hα, at {halphaNm} nm, the thin layer above the surface appears: jets at the limb, bright plage, a prominence standing in the field.

eruption.title: Rise and reconnection
eruption.body: In this reduced cross-section, incoming contours reconnect into rising upper contours and contracting lower loops with fixed footpoints. Dots trace one chosen illustrative plasma flow. Real eruptions are three-dimensional and can change their footpoint connections.

corona.title: Hotter above
corona.body: Typical coronal plasma reaches {coronaMK} million kelvin. Dissipation of waves and magnetic reconnection are supported heating processes; their relative contributions vary and remain under study. Arches and plumes trace some of the magnetic structure.

cycle.title: Eleven years
cycle.body: Spot emergence shifts toward the equator over roughly {cycleYears} years. Polar fields usually reverse near maximum, often at different times in the two hemispheres. This repeating model illustrates the pattern; it does not predict a future cycle.

technicalDetails.title: Inside the Sun lab
technicalDetails.summary: An educational model combines a historical solar interior, processed imagery and procedural structures. Spectral views, magnetic evolution and eruption dynamics are approximations with explicit limits, not calibrated observations or a predictive plasma simulation.

features.views: {views} views, from inside the core to the wind, each at its own pace.
features.interior: The interior from a standard solar model, cut open at any depth, with its profile under the probe.
features.surface: Granulation, spots, faculae and limb darkening, with the surface turning differentially.
features.atmosphere: Chromosphere, spicules and prominences in Hα; the corona's streamers and plumes in an eclipse.
features.field: A potential background field and a separate kinematic reconnection demonstration.
features.lights: Approximate spectral views and a synthetic projected magnetogram re-light the scene.
features.cycle: The activity cycle: spots migrating, the dipole flipping, the record since the seventeenth century.

interior.title: Interior
interior.body: The cut shows Model S (1996): temperature, density, pressure, luminosity and hydrogen fraction. Its centre is {coreTemperatureMK} million kelvin and {centralDensity} times water; nearly all luminosity is generated inside {coreRadius} of the radius. The convection zone begins at {tachocline} of the solar radius. A conventional shell random-walk estimate through the model opacity to that boundary gives {photonWalkKyr} thousand years; Mitalas & Sills report {photonWalkLiteratureKyr} using a different solar model. This is neither a thermal transport solution nor the lifetime of an individual photon. Fusion energy uses neutral hydrogen-1 and helium-4 isotope masses, including annihilation and neutrino energy; L/c² describes photon mass loss only.

rotation.title: Rotation
rotation.body: The Snodgrass–Ulrich surface law gives sidereal periods of {equatorDays} days at the equator and {poleDays} when extrapolated to the pole. Below the tachocline this display chooses uniform rotation at the surface law’s spherical mean, not a measured core rotation rate. The shell motion makes shear visible. Recent deep and near-surface dynamo studies reach different conclusions; this drawing does not resolve that debate.

surface.title: Surface
surface.body: The large-scale white-light texture uses processed SDO/HMI continuum imagery near 617.3 nm, mosaicked from 1–22 May 2024; it is not a simultaneous full-sphere observation. Limb darkening and displayed colour are imposed. NOAA regions initialize the synthetic population, then model evolution takes over. Procedural granules, typically {granuleKm} km across and {granuleMin} minutes long, replace the texture close up. Other passbands are synthetic and are not co-temporal AIA observations.

atmosphere.title: Atmosphere
atmosphere.body: The schematic chromosphere is {chromosphereKm} km deep, viewed in Hα at {halphaNm} nm. A Baumbach profile guides the white-light corona’s radial fall-off; its morphology is authored. The assigned {coronaMK} million kelvin is a representative coronal range, not inferred from scattered-light brightness. Spicules, prominences and loops are prescribed forms. Heating, evaporation, cooling and wind acceleration are not solved.

field.title: Magnetic field
field.body: The potential background combines a global source-surface dipole with buried active-region dipoles. Only the global component satisfies the radial source-surface boundary; this is not an extrapolation of an observed magnetogram. Reference fields are {meanFieldMT} mT for quiet regions and up to {spotFieldT} T in spots. A separate evolving flux function defines the eruption in a dimensionless plane. Its contours transfer equal flux into both products; a chosen velocity and localized nonideal term satisfy induction in that reference plane. Momentum, energy and particle acceleration are not solved. The stretched, extruded display preserves illustrated connectivity, not a global three-dimensional resistive-MHD solution. The upper island does not establish that a real CME disconnects from the Sun. Field energy B²V/(2μ₀) is total uniform-field energy; only free energy above a suitable reference field is available for release. Curves and dots are visibility overlays, not measured emission or particle trajectories.

lights.title: Lights
lights.body: The AIA views use representative ion-response peaks and conventional false colours. Log-normal widths, relative peak weights and layer visibility are hand-chosen, not calibrated instrument responses. Several bands respond to both cool and hot plasma; a selected wavelength is not a thermometer. Density, line-of-sight emission measure, abundances and time-dependent calibration are omitted. Hα and He II 304 need optically thick, non-LTE transfer and can be out of ionization equilibrium. Their brightness here is illustrative. White-light coronal scattering is not a temperature measurement. The magnetogram is a synthetic radial field projected along the sight line, not HMI data. GOES labels are assigned examples of peak soft X-ray classes at Earth; no synthetic GOES flux is calculated.

cycle.title: Cycle
cycle.body: Wolf’s relative number R = k(10g + s) weights groups and individual spots. The idealized {cycleYears}-year animation repeats a chosen latitude and polarity pattern; its calendar labels are model dates, not a hindcast or forecast. Real cycles differ in length, amplitude and hemispheric timing. The separate historical plots use SILSO yearly sunspot numbers since 1700 and a group-number reconstruction reaching into the seventeenth century. The {maunderYears}-year Maunder minimum belongs to that earlier reconstruction, whose sampling and calibration are less secure.

limits.title: Limits
limits.body: The scene is an educational synthesis. Cards distinguish sourced observations, historical model values, derived estimates and teaching choices; not every number is measured. No global magnetohydrodynamic evolution, calibrated radiative transfer, event reconstruction or space-weather prediction is computed. Display scale, duration, emission and contrast are chosen for readability. The May 2024 imagery is historical, not a live Sun feed.
